title: The Poet's Three Copies
synopsis: A young poet copied his book of poems by hand, three times.
Tonight the copy for his friend is gone from his desk.
goal: Find the copy Yun Dong-ju made for his friend, and see why his poems matter.

notes: Played under the glass (InspectScene) on Yun's desk: the thick book with a red spine is the one his words describe; the folded note under it is the label, its last word worn.
The blue drop is the water-drop mark of every keeper's note (Haesu's of Case 10 the last one seen); the bottle of blue ink is the near miss the letter rules out ('not ink').

Measured 2026-11-06 on the grid sheet of dorm_room.webp (picture.measuredOn): the blue ink bottle on the left, the two string-tied copies, the thick red-spined book with the folded note under its corner, the desk lamp; no two areas overlap.

notes: The keeper wrote the place as a riddle the old way (Sora's lesson, Case 01): each group by its body part and strength, its vowel by its line and dot, the paper read from the right (columnHeight 2). The note reads 피아노 안: inside the piano.
Two steps stronger is two more lines (Sora's rule, one line a step): the mouth ㅁ, then ㅂ, then ㅍ. ㅂ and ㅁ are the near misses; ㄷ ㅌ ㅅ are decoys of other body parts.
Every letter is the app's text (SyllableBoard): never in a picture.

clueInputs.note: Sora's Lesson Board: the letters copy the mouth; a stronger sound adds a line.
The water-drop note under the dictionary.

learning.objective: 소라의 규칙(a stronger sound adds a line)을 two steps stronger로 넓혀 읽고, 위치 표현(on its right, on top, at the bottom)대로 네 글자를 종이 제자리에 짓는다.

play.title: A Riddle in the King's Letters
story: You unfold the note. The place is a riddle.
The keeper made it the old way, like Sora's lesson.
"Only a person that knows how the letters are made can read it," Yun smiles.
play.letter:
The copy is safe. Read the place the old way.
A stronger sound adds a line. Two steps stronger adds two lines.
Group 1: the mouth, two steps stronger. Only a standing line.
Group 2: the throat. A standing line, with a dot on its right.
Group 3: the tongue on the gums. A flat line, with a dot on top.
Group 4: the throat again, with the same vowel. The tongue on the gums sits at the bottom.
Read from top to bottom. Two groups in each column. The first column is on the right.
play.question: Build each group in its place on the paper. Where is the copy?
hints: Look at Sora's board: which letter copies the mouth?
Two steps stronger is two more lines. Group 1 is at the top right.
play.successMessage: The note reads 피아노 안: inside the piano!
transition: "There is an old piano in the college hall."
You walk there together under the bare trees.

feedback.비아노안: Group 1 is two steps stronger: two more lines, not one.
feedback.미아노안: Group 1 is two steps stronger than the mouth. Add two lines.
feedback.노안피아: The first column is on the right, not on the left.
feedback.피어노안: Group 2's dot is on the right of its line.

learningGoal.title: Reading numbers, places and a language's story

objectives: Find out what language Yun's poems are in.
intro: Late autumn, 1941. You are a guest of a young poet, Yun Dong-ju.
He studies at Yonhi College in Seoul. He graduates this year.
He wanted to print a book of his poems. It could not be printed.
So he copied it by hand, three times.
Tonight the copy for his friend is gone.
play.caseSummary: Miri, a keeper, hid Yun Dong-ju's copy for his friend inside the college piano. Yun wrote his poems in Korean. Korean was being pushed out of the schools. His friend's family hid the copy under their floor. In 1948 it became a book: Sky, Wind, Stars and Poems.

notes: Season 5 Case 11 (PART 10, 2026-11-06). Yun Dong-ju is real; everything he says and does in the case is made up. Miri, the office man checking rooms, the letter box's lock and the piano are made up.

Real outcome kept: three handwritten copies (teacher Lee Yang-ha, friend Jeong Byeong-uk, himself), the friend's copy hidden by his family and published in 1948; the case ends on the checked fact that Yun wrote his poems in Korean when Korean was pushed out of the schools.
No line of his poems is quoted or translated; only the book's title is given in English.
Yonhi College was, as far as known, a men's college in 1941: Miri is a student who helps in the college, not called a Yonhi student (not source-checked; to confirm).
